nodes.name: Injectivity
nodes.statement: (Injectivity of $\mu_{(\lambda,v,s)}$) Let $f,g\in M_{(\lambda,v,s)}$ and assume $\mu_{(\lambda,v,s)}(f)=\mu_{(\lambda,v,s)}(g)$, namely, \begin{align*} &e_{s,t}f\circ(\pi_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,(i,v(i))}^M))_{i\in\lambda} \circ (e_{v(i),u}\pi_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,(i,v(i))})_{(i,u)\in\lambda\times S}\\ =&e_{s,t}g\circ(\pi_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,(i,v(i))}^M))_{i\in\lambda} \circ (e_{v(i),u}\pi_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,(i,v(i))})_{(i,u)\in\lambda\times S} \end{align*} hold for all $t\in S$. Notice that the following two equations hold: The first equation is \begin{align*} &\pi_{(\lambda,v,v(i))}^M\\ =&e_{v(i),v(i)}\circ \pi_{(\lambda,v,v(i))}^M \\ =&\pi_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,(i,v(i)))}^M \circ (e_{v(j),u}\circ \pi_{(\lambda,v,v(j))}^M)_{(j,u)\in\lambda\times S} \end{align*} The second equation is \[ \mathrm{id}_s:=\pi_{(\{s\},\mathrm{id}_{\{s\}},s)}^M=e_{s,s}\pi_{(S,\mathrm{id}_S,s)}^M (e_{s,t})_{t\in S}. \] By these equations injectivity of $\mu_{(\lambda,v,s)}$ is proved as follows: \begin{align*} f &=\mathrm{id}_s\circ f\circ (\pi_{(\lambda,v,v(i))}^M)_{i\in\lambda}\\ &=e_{s,s}\pi_{(S,\mathrm{id},s)}^M (e_{s,t})_{t\in S}\circ f (\pi_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,(i,v(i)))}^M)_{i\in\lambda} \circ (e_{v(j),u}\circ \pi_{(\lambda,v,v(j))}^M)_{(j,u)\in \lambda\times S}\\ &=e_{s,s}\pi_{(S,\mathrm{id},s)}^M (e_{s,t})_{t\in S}\circ g (\pi_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,(i,v(i)))}^M)_{i\in\lambda} \circ (e_{v(j),u}\circ \pi_{(\lambda,v,v(j))}^M)_{(j,u)\in \lambda\times S}\\ &=g. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Injectivity of $\mu$

nodes.name: Surjectivity
nodes.statement: (Surjectivity of $\mu_{(\lambda,v,s)}$) Let $f/\mathclose\sim\in ({\rm H}(M))_{d,(\lambda,v,s)}$. Define $\tilde{f}$ by $\tilde{f}=\pi_{(S,\mathrm{id},s)}^M\circ f\circ (e_{v(i),u}\circ\pi_{(\lambda,v,i)})_{(i,u)\in \lambda\times S}$. Then the following formula holds. \begin{align*} \mu_{(\lambda,v,s)}(\tilde{f}) &=\left((e_{s,t})_{t\in S}\circ \tilde{f}\circ ( \pi_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,(i,v(i)))}^M)_{i\in\lambda}\right)/\mathclose\sim\\ &=\left((e_{s,t})_{t\in S}\circ \pi_{(S,\mathrm{id},s)}^M\circ f\circ (e_{v(i),u}\circ \pi_{(\lambda,v,i)}^M)_{(i,u)\in \lambda\times S}\circ (\pi_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,(i,v(i)))}^M)_{i\in\lambda}\right)/\mathclose\sim\\ &=\left(e_s\circ f\circ (e_{v(i),u}\circ \pi_{(\lambda,v,i)}^M)_{(i,u)\in \lambda\times S}\circ (\pi_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,(i,v(i)))}^M)_{i\in\lambda}\right)/\mathclose\sim\\ &=\left(f\circ (e_{v(i),u}\circ \pi_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,(i,v(i)))}^M)_{(i,u)\in\lambda\times S}\right)/\mathclose\sim\\ &= f/\mathclose\sim. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Surjectivity of $\mu$

nodes.name: Compatibility
nodes.statement: (Compatibility of $\mu$) Let $f\in M_{(\lambda_1,v_1,s)}$ and $g_i\in M_{(\lambda_2,v_2,v_1(i))}$ for $i\in\lambda_1$. Then \begin{align*} &\mu_{(\lambda_2,v_2,s)}(f\circ (g_i)_{i\in\lambda_1})\\ =&\left((e_{s,t})_{t\in S}\circ f\circ (g_i)_{i\in\lambda_1} \circ (\pi_{(\lambda_2\times S,p_2,(j,v_2(j))}^M)_{j\in\lambda_2}\right)/\mathclose\sim\\ =&\left((e_{s,t})_{t\in S}\circ f\circ (e_{v_1(i),v_1(i)}g_i)_{i\in\lambda_1} \circ (\pi_{(\lambda_2\times S,p_2,(j,v_2(j))}^M)_{j\in\lambda_2}\right)/\mathclose\sim\\ =&\left((e_{s,t})_{t\in S}\circ f \circ (\pi_{(\lambda_1\times S,p_2,(i,v_1(i))}^M)_{i\in\lambda_1} \circ (e_{v_1(i),u})_{(i,u)\in\lambda_1\times S}\circ (g_i)_{i\in\lambda_1} \circ (\pi_{(\lambda_2\times S,p_2,(j,v_2(j))}^M)_{j\in\lambda_2}\right)/\mathclose\sim\\ =&\mu_{(\lambda_1,v_1,s)}(f)\circ (\mu_{(\lambda_2,v_2,v_1(i))}(g_i))_{i\in\lambda_1}. \end{align*} We complete the proof of the proposition.
nodes.statement_short: Compatibility of $\mu$

nodes.name: Natural isomorphism A to (H(A))_d
nodes.statement: Let $M,d,e_s,e_{s,t}$ be as in the previous proposition, $A=(A_s)_{s\in S}$ be an $M$-algebra. Then $({\rm H}(A))_d$ is isomorphic to $A$ via an isomorphism $\mu_A$, where \[ \mu_{A,s}:A_s\ni a\mapsto (e_{s,t}(a))_{t\in S}\in ({\rm H}(A))_{d,s}. \] Moreover, $(\mu_A)_{A\in\mathcal{V}(M)}$ is a natural transformation $\mathrm{id}_{\mathrm{Cat}(\mathcal{V}(M))}$ to $[A\mapsto ({\rm H}(A))_d]$.
assumptions: Let $M,d,e_s,e_{s,t}$ be as in the previous proposition, $A=(A_s)_{s\in S}$ be an $M$-algebra.
conclusions: $({\rm H}(A))_d$ is isomorphic to $A$ via an isomorphism $\mu_A$
$(\mu_A)_{A\in\mathcal{V}(M)}$ is a natural transformation $\mathrm{id}_{\mathrm{Cat}(\mathcal{V}(M))}$ to $[A\mapsto ({\rm H}(A))_d]$.
nodes.label: equiv-many

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 6.4
nodes.statement: Let $f\in M_{(\lambda,v,s)}$ and $a_i\in A_{v(i)}$ for $i\in\lambda$. Then \begin{align*} \mu_{(\lambda,v,s)}(f)(\mu_{A,v(i)}(a_i))_{i\in\lambda} &=(e_{s,t})_{t\in S}\circ f\circ (\pi_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,(i,v(i)))})_{i\in\lambda} (e_{v(i),u}(a_i))_{(i,u)\in\lambda\times S}\\ &=(e_{s,t})_{t\in S}\circ f(e_{v(i),v(i)}(a_i))_{i\in\lambda}\\ &=(e_{s,t})_{t\in S}\circ f(a_i)_{i\in\lambda}\\ &=\mu_{A,s}(f(a_i)_{i\in\lambda}). \end{align*} This equation is nothing but the proposition stated. We prove $(\mu_A)_{A\in\mathcal{V}(M)}$ is a natural transformation. Let $A=(A_s)_{s\in S},B=(B_s)_{s\in S}\in \mathcal{V}(M)$ and $\varphi=(\varphi_s)_{s\in S}$ be a homomorphism $A\rightarrow B$. We prove should the diagram \[\xymatrix{ A\ar[r]^{\mu_A} \ar[d]_\varphi& ({\rm H}(A))_d\ar[d]^{({\rm H}(\varphi))_d}\\ B\ar[r]^{\mu_B} & ({\rm H}(B))_d }\] commute. For $s\in S$ and $a\in A_s$, the equation \begin{align*} \mu_{B,s}(\varphi_s(a)) &=(e_{s,t}(\varphi_s(a))_{t\in S}\\ &=(\varphi_t(e_{s,t}(a)))_{t\in S}\\ &={\rm H}(\varphi)(e_{s,t}(a))_{t\in S}\\ &=({\rm H}(\varphi))_{d,s}(\mu_{A,s}(a)) \end{align*} holds. This is nothing but $\mu_B\circ \varphi=({\rm H}(\varphi))_d\circ \mu_A$, thus it is proved that $(\mu_A)_{A\in\mathcal{V}(M)}$ is a natural transformation.
nodes.statement_short: Direct computation of the homomorphism property and a naturality square chase.

nodes.name: Homomorphism
nodes.statement: Let $f\in M_{(\lambda,v,s)}$ and $a_i\in A_{v(i)}$ for $i\in\lambda$. Then \begin{align*} \mu_{(\lambda,v,s)}(f)(\mu_{A,v(i)}(a_i))_{i\in\lambda} &=(e_{s,t})_{t\in S}\circ f\circ (\pi_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,(i,v(i)))})_{i\in\lambda} (e_{v(i),u}(a_i))_{(i,u)\in\lambda\times S}\\ &=(e_{s,t})_{t\in S}\circ f(e_{v(i),v(i)}(a_i))_{i\in\lambda}\\ &=(e_{s,t})_{t\in S}\circ f(a_i)_{i\in\lambda}\\ &=\mu_{A,s}(f(a_i)_{i\in\lambda}). \end{align*} This equation is nothing but the proposition stated.
nodes.statement_short: Homomorphism property of $\mu_A$

nodes.name: Naturality
nodes.statement: We prove $(\mu_A)_{A\in\mathcal{V}(M)}$ is a natural transformation. Let $A=(A_s)_{s\in S},B=(B_s)_{s\in S}\in \mathcal{V}(M)$ and $\varphi=(\varphi_s)_{s\in S}$ be a homomorphism $A\rightarrow B$. We prove should the diagram \[\xymatrix{ A\ar[r]^{\mu_A} \ar[d]_\varphi& ({\rm H}(A))_d\ar[d]^{({\rm H}(\varphi))_d}\\ B\ar[r]^{\mu_B} & ({\rm H}(B))_d }\] commute. For $s\in S$ and $a\in A_s$, the equation \begin{align*} \mu_{B,s}(\varphi_s(a)) &=(e_{s,t}(\varphi_s(a))_{t\in S}\\ &=(\varphi_t(e_{s,t}(a)))_{t\in S}\\ &={\rm H}(\varphi)(e_{s,t}(a))_{t\in S}\\ &=({\rm H}(\varphi))_{d,s}(\mu_{A,s}(a)) \end{align*} holds. This is nothing but $\mu_B\circ \varphi=({\rm H}(\varphi))_d\circ \mu_A$, thus it is proved that $(\mu_A)_{A\in\mathcal{V}(M)}$ is a natural transformation.
nodes.statement_short: Naturality of $\mu$

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 6.5
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{clone-single} and \ref{clone-many}, there is natural correspondence between many-sorted pure clones and single-sorted clones with diagonal operations (that can be extended to diagonal pair).
nodes.statement_short: Combine Propositions 6.1 and 6.3.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 6.6
nodes.statement: Proposition \ref{many-single},\ref{single-many},\ref{equiv-single} and \ref{equiv-many}, many-sorted varieties are essentially equivalent to single-sorted varieties that have diagonal pairs.
nodes.statement_short: Combine the functors of Propositions 3.5, 5.7 and natural isomorphisms 6.2, 6.4.

nodes.name: Correspondence between pure many-sorted clones and clones with diagonal operations
nodes.statement: Let $\kappa$ be infinite cardinal and $S$ be a cardinal that $0<S<\kappa$. Then $(C,d)\mapsto C_d$ is one to one correspondence between (isomorphism classes of) single-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clones with $S$-ary diagonal operations and (isomorphism classes of) $S$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary pure clones. The converse correspondence is given by $M\mapsto ({\rm H}(M),(\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(s,s))})_{s\in S})$.
assumptions: Let $\kappa$ be infinite cardinal and $S$ be a cardinal that $0<S<\kappa$.
conclusions: $(C,d)\mapsto C_d$ is one to one correspondence between (isomorphism classes of) single-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clones with $S$-ary diagonal operations and (isomorphism classes of) $S$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary pure clones.
The converse correspondence is given by $M\mapsto ({\rm H}(M),(\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(s,s))})_{s\in S})$.
nodes.statement_short: Heterogenization and homogenization give a bijection between clones with $S$-ary diagonal operations and $S$-sorted pure clones.

nodes.name: Clone with a diagonal operation
nodes.statement: Here, a $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone with an $S$-ary diagonal operation means a tuple $(C,d)$ that $C$ is a $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone, $d\in C_S$ and there exists $(e_s)_{s\in S}$ such that $(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})$ is a diagonal pair of $C$.

nodes.name: Isomorphism of clones with diagonal operations
nodes.statement: Clones with diagonal operations $(C,d),(C',d')$ are said to be isomorphic if there is an clone isomorphism $\varphi:C\rightarrow C'$ such that $\varphi(d)=d'$.

nodes.name: Concrete categorical equivalence of many-sorted and single-sorted varieties
nodes.statement: Let $\kappa$ be infinite cardinal, $S$ be a cardinal that $0<S<\kappa$, $M$ be an $S$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone. Then there exists a categorical equivalence $\nu:\mathcal{V}(M)\rightarrow \mathcal{V}({\rm H}(M))$ such that the following diagram commute. \[\xymatrix{ \mathcal{V}(M)\ar[r]^\nu \ar[d]_F& \mathcal{V}({\rm H}(M))\ar[d]^G\\ {\textbf{{\rm Set}}}^S \ar[r]^\varphi & {\cal D}_S }\] The vertical arrow $F$ is the forgetful functors attaining the underlying family of sets. $G$ is the forgetful functor determined by the clone homomorphism $d\in C_{{\cal D}_S}$ maps to $(\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(s,s))}^M)_{s\in S}$. The lower horizontal arrow $\varphi$ is the functor described in Proposition \ref{pureset-and-sets}
assumptions: Let $\kappa$ be infinite cardinal, $S$ be a cardinal that $0<S<\kappa$, $M$ be an $S$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone.
conclusions: there exists a categorical equivalence $\nu:\mathcal{V}(M)\rightarrow \mathcal{V}({\rm H}(M))$ such that the following diagram commute.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal{V}(M)$ is categorically equivalent to $\mathcal{V}({\rm H}(M))$ compatibly with the forgetful functors and $\mathbf{Set}^S\simeq\mathcal{D}_S$.
nodes.label: main-theorem-categorical-equivalence

nodes.name: Many-sorted subalgebra and congruence
nodes.statement: Let $A=(A_s)_{s\in S}$ be an $S$-sorted algebra. \begin{enumerate} \item A subalgebra of $A$ is an $S$-sorted family $B=(B_s)_{s\in S}$ that satisfies the following conditions: \begin{itemize} \item $B_s\subset A_s$ for all $s\in S$. \item For $(\lambda,v)$-ary $s$-valued term operation $f$ of $A$ and $(b_i)_{i\in\lambda}\in \prod_{i\in\lambda}B_{v(i)}$, $f(b_i)_{i\in \lambda}\in B_s$ holds. \end{itemize} The set of all subalgebras of $A$ is denoted by $\mathrm{Sub}(A)$. \item A congruence of $A$ is a subalgebra $(\theta_s)_{s\in S}$ of $A^2=(A_s{}^2)_{s\in S}$ such that $\theta_s$ is an equivalence relation on $A_s$ for each $s\in S$. The set of all congruences of $A$ is denoted by $\mathrm{Con}(A)$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Subalgebras and congruences under homogenization
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be an $S$-sorted clone, $A$ be an $M$-algebra. \begin{enumerate} \item If $B=(B_s)_{s\in S}\in \mathrm{Sub}(A)$, then ${\rm H}(B):=\prod_{s\in S}B_s\in \mathrm{Sub}({\rm H}(A))$. Conversely, Any subalgebra of ${\rm H}(A)$ is described as in the form ${\rm H}(B)$ by $B\in\mathrm{Sub}(A)$. \item If $\theta=(\theta_s)_{s\in S}\in\mathrm{Con}(A)$, then \[ {\rm H}(\theta):=\prod_{s\in S}\theta_s :=\{((a_s)_{s\in S},(b_s)_{s\in S})\in ({\rm H}(A))^2\mid \forall s\in S;(a_s,b_s)\in\theta_s\} \in\mathrm{Con}({\rm H}(A)). \] Conversely, Any congruence of ${\rm H}(A)$ is described as in the form ${\rm H}(\theta)$ by a congruence $\theta\in\mathrm{Con}(A)$. \item If $\theta\in \mathrm{Con}(A)$, then ${\rm H}(A/\theta){\simeq} {\rm H}(A)/{\rm H}(\theta)$. \item If $(A_i)_{i\in I}$ is a family of $M$-algebras, then \[ \prod_{i\in I}{\rm H}(A_i){\simeq} {\rm H}\left(\prod_{i\in I} A_i\right). \] \end{enumerate}
assumptions: Let $M$ be an $S$-sorted clone, $A$ be an $M$-algebra.
conclusions: ${\rm H}(B):=\prod_{s\in S}B_s\in \mathrm{Sub}({\rm H}(A))$
Any subalgebra of ${\rm H}(A)$ is described as in the form ${\rm H}(B)$ by $B\in\mathrm{Sub}(A)$.
Any congruence of ${\rm H}(A)$ is described as in the form ${\rm H}(\theta)$ by a congruence $\theta\in\mathrm{Con}(A)$.
${\rm H}(A/\theta){\simeq} {\rm H}(A)/{\rm H}(\theta)$.
\[ \prod_{i\in I}{\rm H}(A_i){\simeq} {\rm H}\left(\prod_{i\in I} A_i\right). \]
nodes.statement_short: Homogenization matches subalgebras, congruences, quotients and products of $A$ with those of ${\rm H}(A)$.
nodes.label: sub-con-corresopndence

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 7.2
nodes.statement: We only show that any subalgebra of ${\rm H}(A)$ is in the form ${\rm H}(B)$ by a subalgebra $B$ of $A$. Other parts are easily verified or proved similarly. If ${\rm H}(A)= \emptyset$, then the assertion is trivial. Thus, we assume $A_s\neq\emptyset$ for all $s\in S$. Let $B'$ be a subalgebra of ${\rm H}(A)$. Define \[ B_s:=\{b\in A_s\mid\exists (a_t)_{t\in S\setminus\{s\}}\in\prod_{t\in S\setminus\{s\}}A_t; (b,(a_t)_{t\in S\setminus\{s\}})\in B'\}. \] Clearly, $B'\subset \prod_{s\in S}B_s$ holds. We show $\prod_{s\in S}B_s\subset B'$. Let $(b_s)_{s\in S}\in \prod_{s\in S}B_s$. By definition of $B_s$, there exist $(c_{st})_{t\in S}\in B'$ such that $c_{ss}=b_s$. Let $d=(\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(s,s))})_{s\in S}$ be the diagonal term. Then \[ B'\ni d((c_{st})_{t\in s})_{s\in S}=(c_{ss})_{s\in S}=(b_s)_{s\in s}. \qedhere \]
nodes.statement_short: Only the subalgebra correspondence is shown: project a subalgebra of ${\rm H}(A)$ to sorts and recombine with the diagonal term.

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement: We only show that any subalgebra of ${\rm H}(A)$ is in the form ${\rm H}(B)$ by a subalgebra $B$ of $A$. Other parts are easily verified or proved similarly.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the subalgebra statement

nodes.name: Nonempty case
nodes.statement: If ${\rm H}(A)= \emptyset$, then the assertion is trivial. Thus, we assume $A_s\neq\emptyset$ for all $s\in S$.
nodes.statement_short: Dispose of the empty case

nodes.name: Define B_s
nodes.statement: Let $B'$ be a subalgebra of ${\rm H}(A)$. Define \[ B_s:=\{b\in A_s\mid\exists (a_t)_{t\in S\setminus\{s\}}\in\prod_{t\in S\setminus\{s\}}A_t; (b,(a_t)_{t\in S\setminus\{s\}})\in B'\}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Define sort projections $B_s$ of $B'$

nodes.name: Inclusion
nodes.statement: Clearly, $B'\subset \prod_{s\in S}B_s$ holds. We show $\prod_{s\in S}B_s\subset B'$.
nodes.statement_short: One inclusion is clear; reduce to the other

nodes.name: Witnesses
nodes.statement: Let $(b_s)_{s\in S}\in \prod_{s\in S}B_s$. By definition of $B_s$, there exist $(c_{st})_{t\in S}\in B'$ such that $c_{ss}=b_s$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick witnesses $c_{st}$

nodes.name: Diagonal
nodes.statement: Let $d=(\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(s,s))})_{s\in S}$ be the diagonal term. Then \[ B'\ni d((c_{st})_{t\in s})_{s\in S}=(c_{ss})_{s\in S}=(b_s)_{s\in s}. \qedhere \]
nodes.statement_short: Apply the diagonal term to the witnesses

nodes.name: Subalgebra correspondence is bijective for pure clones
nodes.statement: If $M$ is a pure clone, then the underlying family of sets of any subalgebra of an $M$-algebra $A$ is pure. In such case, the correspondence $B\mapsto {\rm H}(B)$ between $\mathrm{Sub}(A)$ and $\mathrm{Sub}({\rm H}(A))$ is bijective. On the other hand, this correspondence may not be bijective if $M$ is not pure. For a simple example, $S=2=\{0,1\}$, $M$ be the trivial $2$-sorted clone (that is, the $2$-sorted clone only consists of projection constants) and $A=(A_i)_{i\in 2}=(A_0,A_1)$, then the both $(\emptyset,A_1)$ and $(A_0,\emptyset)$ of members of $\mathrm{Sub}(A)$ correspond to $\emptyset=\emptyset\times A_1=A_0\times\emptyset$.
nodes.statement_short: For a pure clone the subalgebra correspondence is bijective; a trivial 2-sorted clone shows it can fail otherwise.
nodes.label: subalgebra-of-pure-algebra

nodes.name: Many-sorted Birkhoff variety theorem
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be an $S$-sorted pure clone, $\mathcal{K}$ be a class of $M$-algebras. Then the variety $\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{K})$ generated by $\mathcal{K}$ coincides with $\mathbf{HSP}(\mathcal{K})$.
assumptions: Let $M$ be an $S$-sorted pure clone, $\mathcal{K}$ be a class of $M$-algebras.
conclusions: the variety $\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{K})$ generated by $\mathcal{K}$ coincides with $\mathbf{HSP}(\mathcal{K})$.
nodes.label: variety-theorem

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 7.4
nodes.statement: We show \begin{equation} {\rm H}(\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{K}))=\mathcal{V}({\rm H}(\mathcal{K}))=\mathbf{HSP}({\rm H}(\mathcal{K}))={\rm H}(\mathbf{HSP}(\mathcal{K})). \end{equation} The second equality is Birkhoff's variety theorem for classes of single-sorted algebras. The last equality follows from Proposition \ref{sub-con-corresopndence}. The first equality is proved as follows. For $f,g\in {\rm H}_\lambda(M)$, where $f=(f_s)_{s\in S}$, $g=(g_s)_{s\in S}$, the following equivalence holds: \begin{align*} {\rm H}(\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{K}))\models f=g \Longleftrightarrow& \forall s\in S;\ \mathcal{V}(\mathcal{K})\models f_s=g_s\\ \Longleftrightarrow& \forall s\in S;\ \mathcal{K}\models f_s=g_s\\ \Longleftrightarrow& {\rm H}(\mathcal{K})\models f=g\\ \Longleftrightarrow& \mathcal{V}({\rm H}(\mathcal{K}))\models f=g. \end{align*} It means the equational theories defining $\mathcal{V}({\rm H}(\mathcal{K}))$ and ${\rm H}(\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{K}))$ coincide with each other. Therefore, ${\rm H}(\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{K}))=\mathcal{V}({\rm H}(\mathcal{K}))$ holds. By (\ref{varieties-through-homogenization}) and Theorem \ref{main-theorem-categorical-equivalence}, $\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{K})=\mathbf{HSP}(\mathcal{K})$ holds.
nodes.statement_short: Transfer through homogenization: chain of equalities using Birkhoff's single-sorted theorem and Proposition 7.2, then the categorical equivalence.

nodes.name: Varieties through homogenization
nodes.statement: {\rm H}(\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{K}))=\mathcal{V}({\rm H}(\mathcal{K}))=\mathbf{HSP}({\rm H}(\mathcal{K}))={\rm H}(\mathbf{HSP}(\mathcal{K})).
nodes.label: varieties-through-homogenization

nodes.name: Goal
nodes.statement: We show \begin{equation} {\rm H}(\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{K}))=\mathcal{V}({\rm H}(\mathcal{K}))=\mathbf{HSP}({\rm H}(\mathcal{K}))={\rm H}(\mathbf{HSP}(\mathcal{K})). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: State the chain of equalities to prove

nodes.name: Birkhoff
nodes.statement: The second equality is Birkhoff's variety theorem for classes of single-sorted algebras.
nodes.statement_short: Second equality by Birkhoff's theorem

nodes.name: Last equality
nodes.statement: The last equality follows from Proposition \ref{sub-con-corresopndence}.
nodes.statement_short: Last equality by Proposition 7.2

nodes.name: First equality
nodes.statement: The first equality is proved as follows. For $f,g\in {\rm H}_\lambda(M)$, where $f=(f_s)_{s\in S}$, $g=(g_s)_{s\in S}$, the following equivalence holds: \begin{align*} {\rm H}(\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{K}))\models f=g \Longleftrightarrow& \forall s\in S;\ \mathcal{V}(\mathcal{K})\models f_s=g_s\\ \Longleftrightarrow& \forall s\in S;\ \mathcal{K}\models f_s=g_s\\ \Longleftrightarrow& {\rm H}(\mathcal{K})\models f=g\\ \Longleftrightarrow& \mathcal{V}({\rm H}(\mathcal{K}))\models f=g. \end{align*} It means the equational theories defining $\mathcal{V}({\rm H}(\mathcal{K}))$ and ${\rm H}(\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{K}))$ coincide with each other. Therefore, ${\rm H}(\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{K}))=\mathcal{V}({\rm H}(\mathcal{K}))$ holds.
nodes.statement_short: First equality: equational theories coincide

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: By (\ref{varieties-through-homogenization}) and Theorem \ref{main-theorem-categorical-equivalence}, $\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{K})=\mathbf{HSP}(\mathcal{K})$ holds.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude via the categorical equivalence

nodes.name: Equivalence with the usual variety theorem
nodes.statement: As noted in preliminary section, the above clone-based formulation includes type-based formulation as the case that $M$ is a free clone. Thus, Theorem \ref{variety-theorem} above is essentially equivalent to usual formulation of variety theorem.

nodes.name: Denecke-Lueders theorem
nodes.statement: Denecke and L\"{u}ders proved in \cite{DL} that two finite single-sorted algebras are categorically equivalent if and only if their relational clones are isomorphic.
assumptions: two finite single-sorted algebras
conclusions: two finite single-sorted algebras are categorically equivalent if and only if their relational clones are isomorphic.

nodes.name: Relational clone of a many-sorted algebra
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be an $S$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary algebra, $\kappa'$ be a cardinal. A $<\mathclose\kappa'$-ary relational clone of $A$ is the family $\mathrm{Inv}_{<\mathclose\kappa'}(A)=(\mathrm{Inv}_\mu(A))_{\mu<\kappa'}$, where $\mathrm{Inv}_\mu(A)=\{{\rm H}(B)\mid B\in\mathrm{Sub}(A)\}$, namely, $\mathrm{Inv}_\mu(A)$ is the set of all subsets $r$ of $\left(\prod_{s\in S}A_s\right)^\mu$ that satisfy \begin{align*} &f_s\in \mathrm{Clo}_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,s)}(A),(a_{i,j,t})_{(t,j)\in S\times\mu}\in r\ (\text{for }i\in\lambda)\\ \Longrightarrow& (f_s(a_{i,j,t})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S})_{(s,j)\in S\times\mu}\in r. \end{align*} Here, $\mathrm{Clo}_{(\lambda,v,s)}(A)$ is the set of all $(\lambda,v)$-ary $s$-valued term operations of $A$. A member of $\mathrm{Inv}_\mu(A)$ is said an $\mu$-ary invariant set of $A$.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathrm{Inv}_\mu(A)$: subsets of $(\prod_sA_s)^\mu$ closed under the componentwise action of term operations.

nodes.name: Sort-wise closed relations
nodes.statement: We can consider the set of all closed subsets for component-wise operations. Here, a set $r\subset \prod_{j\in\mu}A_{v(j)}$ ($\mu$ is a cardinal, $v:\mu\rightarrow S$) is said closed if the following condition holds: For $\mu<\kappa'$ and $v:\mu\rightarrow S$ \begin{align*} &f_j\in \mathrm{Clo}_{(\lambda,[i\mapsto v(j)],v(j))}(A),(a_{i,j})_{j\in\mu}\in r\ (\text{for }i\in\lambda)\\ \Longrightarrow& (f_j(a_{i,j})_{i\in\lambda})_{j\in\mu}\in r. \end{align*} However, this condition considers only on operations related at most one sort. Thus, it should be said a concept of the non-indexed product of an one-sorted algebras, rather than a concept of a many-sorted algebra.
nodes.statement_short: Relations closed only under sort-wise operations describe a non-indexed product of one-sorted algebras, not a many-sorted algebra.

nodes.name: Relational clone of an algebra equals that of its homogenization
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be an $S$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary pure clone, $A$ be an $M$-algebra, and $\kappa'$ be an arbitrary cardinal. Then the $<\mathclose\kappa'$-ary relational clone $\mathrm{Inv}_{<\kappa'}(A)$ is isomorphic to $\mathrm{Inv}_{<\kappa'}({\rm H}(A))$.
assumptions: Let $M$ be an $S$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary pure clone, $A$ be an $M$-algebra, and $\kappa'$ be an arbitrary cardinal.
conclusions: the $<\mathclose\kappa'$-ary relational clone $\mathrm{Inv}_{<\kappa'}(A)$ is isomorphic to $\mathrm{Inv}_{<\kappa'}({\rm H}(A))$.
nodes.label: many-single-relationa-clone

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 7.10
nodes.statement: By the definition of homogenization and relational clone, \[ \mathrm{Inv}_\mu(A)\ni r\mapsto \{((a_{j,s})_{s\in S})_{j\in\mu}\in ({\rm H}(A))^\mu\mid(a_{j,s})_{(j,s)\in\mu\times S}\in r\} \in \mathrm{Inv}_{\mu}({\rm H}(A)) \] is an isomorphism of relational clone. Note that the bijectivity of this correspondence follows from pureness of $M$ (Remark \ref{subalgebra-of-pure-algebra}).
nodes.statement_short: Regroup coordinates to map invariant sets of $A$ to those of ${\rm H}(A)$; bijectivity uses pureness.

nodes.name: Many-sorted categorical equivalence via relational clones
nodes.statement: Let $S_k$ be a non-zero cardinal, $\kappa$ be an infinite cardinal that $S_k<\kappa$ for $k=1,2$. Let $A_k$ be an $S_k$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary algebra that the clones of term operations are pure for $k=1,2$. Let $\kappa'$ be an infinite cardinal that satisfies \[ \lambda<\kappa\ \Longrightarrow |A_1|^\lambda, |A_2|^\lambda <\kappa', \] where $|A_k|$ is the product cardinal $\prod_{s\in S_k} |A_{k,s}|$. Then the following assertions are equivalent. \begin{enumerate} \item There exists a categorical equivalence $\mathcal{V}(A_1)\rightarrow\mathcal{V}(A_2)$ that maps $A_1$ to $A_2$. \item The relational clones $\mathrm{Inv}_{<\mathclose\kappa'}(A_1)$ is isomorphic to $\mathrm{Inv}_{<\mathclose\kappa'}(A_2)$. \end{enumerate}
assumptions: Let $S_k$ be a non-zero cardinal, $\kappa$ be an infinite cardinal that $S_k<\kappa$ for $k=1,2$.
Let $A_k$ be an $S_k$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary algebra that the clones of term operations are pure for $k=1,2$.
Let $\kappa'$ be an infinite cardinal that satisfies \[ \lambda<\kappa\ \Longrightarrow |A_1|^\lambda, |A_2|^\lambda <\kappa', \]
conclusions: the following assertions are equivalent.
equivalent_conditions: There exists a categorical equivalence $\mathcal{V}(A_1)\rightarrow\mathcal{V}(A_2)$ that maps $A_1$ to $A_2$.
The relational clones $\mathrm{Inv}_{<\mathclose\kappa'}(A_1)$ is isomorphic to $\mathrm{Inv}_{<\mathclose\kappa'}(A_2)$.
nodes.statement_short: Two many-sorted algebras with pure term clones are categorically equivalent iff their relational clones are isomorphic.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 7.11
nodes.statement: This corollary follows from Theorem \ref{main-theorem-categorical-equivalence}, Theorem \ref{many-single-relationa-clone} and the following theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Combine Theorems 6.6 and 7.10 with the single-sorted Theorem 7.12.

nodes.name: Categorical equivalence of infinitary algebras via relational clones
nodes.statement: Let $\kappa$ be an infinite cardinal and $A_k$ be a single-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary algebra for $k=1,2$. Let $\kappa'$ be an infinite cardinal that satisfies $\lambda<\kappa\ \Longrightarrow |A_1|^\lambda,|A_2|^\lambda<\kappa'$. Then the following assertions are equivalent. \begin{enumerate} \item There exists a categorical equivalence $\mathcal{V}(A_1)\rightarrow\mathcal{V}(A_2)$ that maps $A_1$ to $A_2$. \item The relational clones $\mathrm{Inv}_{<\mathclose\kappa'}(A_1)$ is isomorphic to $\mathrm{Inv}_{<\mathclose\kappa'}(A_2)$. \end{enumerate}

Let $\kappa'$ be an infinite cardinal that satisfies $\lambda<\kappa\ \Longrightarrow |A_1|^\lambda,|A_2|^\lambda<\kappa'$.

nodes.name: Congruence permutability
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be an $S$-sorted algebra. \begin{enumerate} \item Let $\theta_s,\eta_s\subset A_s{}^2$. A relational product $\theta\circ\eta$ of $\theta=(\theta_s)_{s\in S}$ and $\eta=(\eta_s)_{s\in S}$ is defined by sort-wise relational product $(\theta_s\circ\eta_s)_{s\in S}$. \item An algebra $A$ is said congruence permutable if $\theta\circ\eta=\eta\circ\theta$ for all $\theta,\eta\in\mathrm{Con}(A)$. \item A class of algebras $\mathcal{K}$ is said congruence permutable if all members of $\mathcal{K}$ are congruence permutable. \end{enumerate}

Then the following conditions are equivalent. \begin{enumerate} \item $\mathcal{V}(M)$ is congruence permutable. \item $\mathcal{V}({\rm H}(M))$ is congruence permutable. \item There exists $p\in {\rm H}_3(M)$, called Mal'cev term, that satisfies \[ p(\pi_{(3,0)},\pi_{(3,0)},\pi_{(3,1)})=\pi_{(3,1)} ,p(\pi_{(3,0)},\pi_{(3,1)},\pi_{(3,1)})=\pi_{(3,0)}, \] where $3$ is a three elements set $\{0,1,2\}$. \item For each $s\in S$, there exists $p_s\in M_{(3\times S,p_2,s)}$ such that \begin{align*} p_s((\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(0,t))})_{t\in S},(\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(0,t))})_{t\in S},(\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(1,t))})_{t\in S}) =\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(1,t))},\\ p_s((\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(0,t))})_{t\in S},(\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(1,t))})_{t\in S},(\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(1,t))})_{t\in S}) =\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(0,t))}. \end{align*} \item For each $s\in S$, there exists $p_s\in M_{3s\rightarrow s}$ such that \begin{align*} p_s(\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,0)},\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,0)},\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,1)}) =\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,1)},\\ p_s(\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,0)},\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,1)},\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,1)}) =\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,0)}. \end{align*} \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 7.14
nodes.statement: 1 $\Leftrightarrow$ 2 is an easy consequence of Proposition \ref{sub-con-corresopndence}. 2 $\Leftrightarrow$ 3 is well known Mal'cev's theorem (See e.g.{\cite[Theorem 12.2]{BS}}). 3 $\Leftrightarrow$ 4 follows from the definition of homogenization. 5 $\Rightarrow$ 4 is trivial. 1 $\Rightarrow$ 5. Let $F$ be a rank $(3\delta_{st})_{t\in S}$ free algebra, namely, there are three elements $a,b,c$ of sort $s$ such that $\{a,b,c\}$ freely generates $F$. Let $\theta$ and $\eta$ be congruences of $F$ generated by $(a,b)$ and $(b,c)$ respectively. (Intuitively, $d$ and $e_n$ are the operations such that $d:((a_{ij})_{j\in \mathbb{N}})_{i\in \mathbb{N}}\mapsto (a_{jj})_{j\in \mathbb{N}}$ and \mbox{$e_n:(a_i)_{i\in\mathbb{N}}\mapsto (a_n,(u)_{i\in\mathbb{N}\setminus\{n\}})$}.) nodes.name: Proof of Example 7.17
nodes.statement: 1. Each $C_n$ has J\'onsson term, thus $\mathcal{V}(C_n)$ is congruence distributive. Thus, \[ \mathcal{V}(C)=\mathcal{V}\left(\prod_{n\in\mathbb{N}}C_n\right){\simeq} \bigotimes_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\mathcal{V}(C_n) \] is congruence distributive. Here, $\otimes_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\mathcal{V}(C_n)$ denotes non-indexed product of the family $\{\mathcal{V}(C_n)\}_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ of varieties. By Proposition \ref{sub-con-corresopndence}, $\mathcal{V}(C_d)$ also be congruence distributive. 2. If $C$ has J\'onsson term of length $n$, then $C_{n+1}$ also has J\'onsson term of length $n$. It is verified by the induction on $n$ that this is impossible. 3. It is easily verified that $e_n(C)$ is isomorphic to $C_n$. Particularly, $e_n(C)$ has J\'onsson term. These are nothing but the terms of $C_d$ satisfying Condition 6 of the theorem. 4. Let $f\in C_{d,(\aleph_0,v,n)}$, where $v:\aleph_0\rightarrow \mathbb{N}$ and $n\in\mathbb{N}$. By the definition of heterogenization, $f$ is represented by $\tilde{f}\in C_{\aleph_0}$ such that $e_n\circ\tilde{f}=\tilde{f}$. This condition implies that the $n$-th component of $\tilde{f}$ is an element of $C_n$ (it is finitary), and other components are $u$ (depend no variables). Therefore, $\tilde{f}$, particularly $f$, is finitary.
